## Reviewer 2

**Comment 1:** The paper is focused on demand censoring of contraceptive products in FPSC in low-income countries, which commonly arise as a result of stockouts and service interruptions. This demand censoring in turn causes biased forecasts in future periods that subsequently culminate in additional cycles of stockouts and unmet need for clients. Within this context, the paper proposes a forecasting method named the truncated conformal Kalman filter (TCKF), which aims to improve the forecasting accuracy of contraceptive demand at health facilities. The performance of the proposed method is tested and compared with state-of-the-art forecasting methodologies using (i) a numerical experiment involving synthetic data, and (ii) an empirical experiment involving real-world data from the family planning supply chain in Côte d’Ivoire. The paper claims that the proposed TCKF methodology outperforms others with respect to forecasting accuracy, inventory outcomes (i.e., cycle service level, stock-out, and inventory turnover), as well as public health outcomes (e.g., modern contraceptive prevalence rate, unintended pregnancies, infant deaths).

Overall, the paper is focused on a very important and relevant topic, with consequential implications for public health in low-income countries. I applaud the authors for selecting such a topic. In what follows, I highlight my key concerns along with suggestions for improvements.

**Response:** Thank you for this positive summary and for recognising the importance of the problem setting and its public-health implications. We deeply appreciate your constructive feedback, which has been instrumental in strengthening both the theoretical rigor and the practical relevance of this work.

In this revision, we have carefully addressed all of the concerns raised throughout your review and have fully incorporated your suggested improvements. All substantive changes have been implemented and are clearly highlighted in the revised document. Given the substantial volume of these revisions, we have opted not to reproduce the entirety of the newly drafted text and figures within the body of this letter to ensure it remains concise and easily navigable. Instead, we kindly invite you to refer to the specific sections of the main manuscript and the E-Companion referenced under each of our detailed responses below.

**Comment 2:** In Equation (17), the paper develops a composite metric of inventory performance which combines (i) cycle service level (i.e., stock-in rate), (ii) stock-out rate, and (iii) inventory turnover (i.e., which is a proxy for overstocking) by assigning equal weights, for which no convincing justification—based on either theory or practice—is provided. In practice, however, the first two metrics should generally be weighted higher than overstocking (note that this choice needs to be driven by data). It is true that overstocking incurs holding and obsolescence costs, but these are likely to be significantly discounted against the opportunity cost of lost demand, which translate into much more severe repercussions for clients (e.g., mortality).

This is a key limitation of the paper when it comes to comparing the performance of TCKF to other methods. I suspect if the paper were to assume greater weights for service level and stockout, their proposed framework may no longer be the overall top performer. For example, that TCKF seems to be performing well on avoiding overstocking, but it is outperformed by local “demand planner” and “system generated” forecasts when it comes to maintaining high service levels and avoiding stockouts (see Table 6). This is interesting as it shows that local agents with in-depth on-the-ground knowledge also assign a significantly higher weight to service level and stockouts and discount overstocking. Perhaps the local agents do take into account real-world uncertainties that TCKF does not account for. Relatedly, the paper claims in multiple areas that “high levels of overstocking are operationally inefficient and may divert stock away from other sites in need”. However, this claim needs to be grounded in field evidence and data. Otherwise, it runs the risk of appearing speculative. More importantly, the operational cost of overstocking must be juxtaposed against the opportunity cost of stockouts whenever these appear side-by-side.

**Response:** Thank you for this constructive comment. We agree that the previous equal-weight composite metric was insufficiently justified, and that in public health supply chains, the severe human repercussions of stockouts must be weighted far more heavily than the holding costs of overstocking. 

To address these, we have made substantial revisions to our evaluation framework and narrative:

- We removed the equal-weight composite metric entirely. Instead, we introduce the URS, a unified quadratic (L2 norm) cost function that explicitly juxtaposes the opportunity cost of stockouts against the operational burden of overstocking. To test higher service-level weights, we evaluated all models across a grid of trade-off settings (from $w=0.10$ to $w=0.90$).

- You rightly observed that local Demand Planners achieve exceptionally high service levels (CSL = 0.99). We have expanded our discussion to engage with this behavioural divergence. Planners do indeed recognise the severe asymmetric penalty of stockouts and attempt to manually buffer against them. However, our expanded empirical analysis reveals that they achieve this 0.99 CSL via unsustainable hoarding, requiring a normalised inventory footprint of 12.82 (almost 13 months of supply). By contrast, TCKF achieves highly competitive service levels (0.92 CSL) with a mathematically optimal footprint (4.63), maintaining robust probabilistic coverage without relying on prohibitive excess stock.

- We also revised the discussion of overstocking. Rather than making speculative claims, we now ground the narrative in field evidence and prior work: in our discussions with supply-chain practitioners (including Ethiopian Pharmaceutical Supply Service (EPSS) and DHIS2 implementers, and former USAID professionals), a consistent theme was that facilities often inflate orders to hedge against upstream uncertainty and resource constraints, where facilities may deliberately prioritise availability even if that implies carrying larger buffers. For example, when the actual need is 100 units, facilities may request substantially more to ensure receipt of at least the required amount. This behaviour can improve service levels but also generates systematic overstocking and uneven resource use across facilities. We therefore interpret planner-adjusted and system-generated forecasts as meaningful operational benchmarks that may embed local risk perceptions, and we evaluate all methods using the same service–inventory trade-off framework.

These changes have been incorporated in *Section 4.3.3*, *Section 5.4*, *Section 5.5*, and *E-companion, Section 6*.

**Comment 3:** On p. 18, it is claimed that “censored Linear Regression achieved the highest CSL and lowest stockout rate among all candidate methods, but this came at the expense of substantial overstocking.” What is meant by substantial overstocking and how is that measured? What is the threshold at which overstocking becomes a problem? Again, this claim appears incomplete without comparing the holding costs of overstocking against the opportunity costs of stockouts.

**Response:**  Thank you for noting this. We agree that the phrase “substantial overstocking” was vague and incomplete without a clear quantitative definition and a formal cost/trade-off context. 

To address your specific questions: we now explicitly define and measure overstocking using the normalised average on-hand inventory ($I_{norm}$), which intuitively represents the months of supply held. In the revised text, we clarify the comparative "threshold" of inefficiency: while Censored Linear Regression achieves a 0.92 CSL, it requires an $I_{norm}$ of 3.25 to do so. TCKF achieves the exact same service level with a significantly leaner footprint ($I_{norm} = 2.75$). 

Furthermore, to compare the holding costs of overstocking against the severe opportunity costs of stockouts, we evaluate all methods using the newly introduced Unified Relative Score (URS). As detailed in our previous responses, the URS explicitly juxtaposes these costs across a spectrum of penalty weights ($w$), demonstrating how excessive inventory buffering is mathematically penalised under realistic operational constraints. 

These changes have been incorporated in *Section 5.4* and *Section 5.5*.

**Comment 4:** Please define the three inventory metrics more upfront rather than in the appendix (the formulas can still be presented in the appendix to save space). Further, are cycle service level and stockout rate simply the opposite of each other? If so, what is the justification for including both in the composite metric?

**Response:** Thank you for pointing this out. We fully agree that burying the metric definitions in the appendix reduced the clarity of the paper, and your observation regarding the redundancy of CSL and the stockout rate is entirely correct. 

To address this, we have made the following specific revisions:

- We have brought the formal definitions and equations for the primary inventory metrics, Cycle Service Level (CSL) and Normalised Average Inventory ($I_{norm}$).

- As noted in our responses above, we have entirely discarded the previous composite metric. In the revised manuscript, our unified objective (the URS) relies strictly on the trade-off between service failures $(1 - CSL)$ and inventory footprint $(I_{norm})$.

-  We now retain the term "Stock-Out Rate" (SOR) and its equation exclusively in Public health indicators. We do this solely for interpretability during the public health translation phase, as established public health impact tools (such as the RHSC Impact Calculator) require stockout rate as their standard input metric. 

These changes have been incorporated in *Section 4.3.2*, *Section 4.3.4* and *E-companion, Section 3 and 4*.

**Comment 5:** In Equation 14 in the Appendix, inventory turnover is defined as the “average stock relative to the target level.” First, what is the target level? I assume it’s the three-month buffer? Second, is inventory turnover the correct terminology given that it could have other connotations? Third, the paper assumes that high inventory turnover is synonymous to overstocking. But it appears that is only the case for inventory turnover values that are above one. For example, the demand planner method may not be suffering from overstocking if inventory turnover is below 1. Please clarify.

**Response:** Thank you for raising this. We agree that the previous appendix definition was unclear about what the “target level” referred to, used the term “inventory turnover” in a potentially misleading way, and could create confusion about when the metric implies overstocking (e.g., values below versus above one). In the revised manuscript, we removed the earlier turnover/target-level formulation and instead evaluate inventory outcomes using a clearer separation: (i) service is measured by cycle service level (and the corresponding stock-out rate), and (ii) the inventory burden required to achieve that service is measured using average on-hand inventory, reported in a normalised form to ensure comparability across products and facilities. We also revised the surrounding text to avoid vague terminology and to present the service–inventory trade-off transparently.

These changes have been incorporated in *Section 4.3.2* and *E-companion, Section 4*.

**Comment 6:** I also wanted to bring up a few other related concerns for author(s)’ consideration. The source of distorted demand figures is currently claimed to be driven solely by partial censorship (stockout) and full censorship (service interruptions). First, this ignores the fact that another source of demand distortion is subpar data collection practices at clinics (e.g., due to lack of training; see Karamshetty et al. 2022), even in the absence of service interruptions. Perhaps you may need to be explicit that your proposed methodology is not designed to account for this source of bias. Second, how do you differentiate between partial and full censorship, especially considering that the latter may cause the former? That is, service interruptions themselves cause stockouts.

**Response:** Thank you for raising these related concerns. We agree that demand distortion can also arise from data quality issues at clinics (e.g., recording/reporting practices), and our methodology is not designed to correct for that type of bias and addressing broader data-quality bias may require additional data audits and modelling. We have now stated this explicitly in the Method section by clarifying the scope of the approach and listing key sources of distortion that are outside our modelling framework.

We also clarified how we distinguish partial and full censoring in our setting. Stockouts and service interruptions are identified using separately recorded operational information in the dataset, and we treat them as distinct mechanisms. In our analysis, service-interruption periods are handled separately and are not conflated with stockout periods, which avoids ambiguity even when interruptions may contribute to later stockouts.

These changes have been incorporated in *Section 3.6*.

**Comment 7:** My other key concern is related to the feasibility and scalability of implementing the proposed approach, assuming that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The paper does not dedicate a whole ton of attention to this matter, but this is consequential in ensuring that the paper’s potential contributions extend beyond theory. To that end, the paper needs to show that the proposed method is something that can be realistically implemented on the ground (feasibility), and not just in a handful of clinics but rather nationwide (scalability). How would the method be implemented at health facilities or regional warehouses? What kind of infrastructure and training is required? How capital intensive is the process? These are all questions that deserve attention.

Based on Figure 10, it seems like the currently used demand planner method is already doing an excellent job in terms of public health metrics, while at the same time having the advantage of parsimony. The question then becomes what are the costs and consequences of replacing this system with TCKF? What does the system gain (benefit) and what price does it have to pay in return (cost)? And is implementing TCKF worth it when considering these benefits and costs? These aspects are not currently discussed in the paper. **[BR and AS - Can you help me to answer this?]**

**Response:** Thank you for raising these critical points. We agree that the practical deployment and operational trade-offs of TCKF must be explicitly justified. To address your concerns, we have expanded our discussion:

- Based on our collaborations with DHIS2 and CHAP, TCKF is designed to be deployed centrally as a backend computational engine. Because it relies entirely on existing LMIS indicators, it requires no capital-intensive infrastructure or new data streams. Facility-level staff simply interact with automated replenishment targets via their current dashboards, requiring zero specialised training.

- You correctly note that Demand Planners achieve an excellent Cycle Service Level (CSL = 0.99). However, our expanded analysis reveals the unsustainable "cost" of this human intervention: planners achieve this via massive inventory hoarding, requiring a footprint of $I_{norm} = 12.82$ (nearly 13 months of supply). In resource-constrained networks, this extreme buffering physically starves other facilities of life-saving commodities. 

These changes have been incorporated in *Section 5.4* and *Section 6.2, 5th Para*.

**Comment 8:** On p. 20, the public health metrics appear to have been calculated incorrectly. Specifically, it is mentioned that “using Censored LightGBM instead of TCKF would correspond to an additional 46,607 women losing access, leading to over 12,800 unintended pregnancies and 186 infant deaths in a hypothetical population of 100,000.” However, based on the conversion factors in the appendix, the correct numbers should be 466, 128 and 1.86, respectively. Further, comparing the TCKF against the worst performing forecasting method does not seem fair. Meanwhile, the performance of the censored linear regression is better than the TCKF and that of the naïve method is almost comparable (see Figure 6).

**Response:** Thank you for carefully checking these calculations and for your critical assessment of our baselines. You are entirely correct that the initial figures were incorrectly scaled, and we sincerely apologise for this oversight. 

We fully agree that benchmarking against the worst-performing model (Censored LightGBM) was an unfair comparison that undermined our results. We have removed this comparison entirely. Instead, we now benchmark TCKF against highly competitive, realistic operational baselines: the *Mean method* (for the numerical experiment) and the actual *System-Generated baseline* (for the empirical experiment).

Next, with the corrected scaling and new baselines, the public health impact remains highly substantial. In the numerical experiment under the 95th-percentile policy, relying on the Mean method results in 2,600 fewer women retaining access per 100,000 population, translating to 716 unintended pregnancies. In the empirical setting, we now contextualise the impact using the actual demographic reality of Côte d’Ivoire (1.59 million women of reproductive age). Here, transitioning from current System-Generated forecasts to TCKF successfully prevents an additional 24,761 women from losing access to contraception, averting 6,821 unintended pregnancies.

Finally, regarding Censored Linear Regression and the Naive method appearing competitive, we have added explicit text to the manuscript to clarify this dynamic. While Censored LR matches TCKF's top-tier service level (CSL = 0.92), it achieves this through overstocking, requiring a normalised inventory footprint ($I_{norm}$) of 3.25. In contrast, TCKF achieves the exact same service level with a significantly leaner footprint ($I_{norm} = 2.75$). Similarly, simple baselines like the Naive method only appear competitive under extreme penalty weights by brute-forcing service levels via massive inventory hoarding. 

These changes have been incorporated in *Section 5.4* and *Section 5.6*.

**Response:** Thank you for noting this. We have revised the text on p.13 to clarify the replenishment process.

These changes have been incorporated in *Section 4.2, 1st para*.

**Comment 10:** On p. 20, it is mentioned that 9 contraceptive products are used in the empirical experiment, but only seven 7 are listed. Relatedly, the numerical experiment is based on 10 contraceptive products, but the names are not listed.

Thank you for pointing this out. We agree the original text was unclear. In the empirical experiment, we analyse nine products that fall within seven contraceptive categories (e.g., male and female condoms are two distinct products within the condom category), and we have revised the manuscript to state this explicitly and align the counts. We also clarified the numerical experiment description: the “10 products” are synthetic product proxies used for the simulation design (rather than named items), and we revised the text to make this explicit.

These changes have been incorporated in *Section 5.2, 1st para*.

*Section 2.4*

**Response:** Thank you for this comment. We revised Section 4.1 to state explicitly that our forecasting target is monthly facility-level product demand, and to clarify the distinction between observed (potentially censored) demand and latent (true) demand.

These changes have been incorporated in *Section 4.1, 2nd para*.

*Comment 14:* In Table 4, a legend may be a good idea to indicate to the reader whether lower vs. higher values are desired in each column.

**Response:** Thank you for the suggestion. We agree that indicating directionality helps readability. In the revised manuscript, we simplified Table 4 to focus on the two core inventory outcomes, CSL and normalised inventory burden (I_norm) and revised the table presentation to make the intended interpretation clearer, while recognising the service–inventory trade-off.

**Comment 15:** On p. 4, it is mentioned that “many tools currently used in FPSC continue to rely on naïve averages or rolling consumption metrics, treating observed demand as complete (USAID, 2000).” However, the referenced citation is from 2000. Please consider including a more recent citation to highlight that “naïve averages or rolling consumption metrics” are still the commonly used practices up to the present day.

**Response:** Thank you for this comment. We agree the original citation was dated. In the revision, we add a recent reference (including [@hewage2025]) to support that rolling-average/consumption-based forecasting remains common practice in FPSC, alongside the original USAID (2000) for context.

These changes have been incorporated in *Section 2.1, 4th Para*.
